recipes.title: Design page layouts and scalable artwork
recipes.description: Match the tool to page layout, vector illustration, everyday documents or programmable typesetting.

picks.label: Print layout
picks.reason: Page layout, color management and PDF output suit brochures and multi-page publications.
picks.tradeoff: Check imported assets and press requirements; proprietary layout-document interchange is limited.

picks.label: Vector artwork
picks.reason: SVG-native editing suits icons, logos and illustrations that must remain scalable.
picks.tradeoff: It is primarily a drawing workflow; complex multi-page publishing needs a layout application.

picks.label: Office documents
picks.reason: Writer, Calc and Impress cover ordinary documents without a separate publishing stack.
picks.tradeoff: Complex imported Office files and macros need compatibility checks.

picks.label: Programmable documents
picks.reason: The open-source compiler and templates support repeatable technical reports.
picks.tradeoff: The markup workflow and hosted-editor plans differ from traditional desktop word processing.

recipes.title: Inspect and process image files

picks.label: RAW photography
picks.reason: Non-destructive processing and image-library tools fit photographic development.
picks.tradeoff: Learn the processing pipeline and verify camera support.

picks.label: Minimal viewing
picks.reason: A sparse viewer interface keeps attention on the image.
picks.tradeoff: It omits full cataloging and photo-editing features.

picks.label: Browse and batch
picks.reason: Viewing, metadata and batch conversion are available in one application.
picks.tradeoff: Company use needs an appropriate paid license.

picks.label: Scripted processing
picks.reason: Command-line transforms support repeatable conversion and image-composition pipelines.
picks.tradeoff: Build options, delegates and security policy affect supported formats.

recipes.title: Trim, convert and inspect media

picks.reason: An FFmpeg-based desktop interface exposes production-oriented conversion and rewrapping.

picks.label: Matroska tracks

picks.label: Diagnose a file

picks.reason: Integrated debugging, terminals, source control, and extensions support many languages in one workspace.
picks.tradeoff: The official Microsoft binary has different terms from the MIT-licensed Code-OSS source; extensions have their own licenses.

picks.label: Custom terminal workflow
picks.reason: Lua configuration and an embeddable API suit users who want to assemble a keyboard-driven environment.
picks.tradeoff: Modal editing and plugin configuration require learning and ongoing choices.

picks.label: Integrated terminal features
picks.reason: Multiple selections, Tree-sitter editing, and built-in LSP support provide a cohesive terminal editing model.
picks.tradeoff: Its selection-first controls differ from Vim and GUI editors.

picks.label: Paid text-editing focus
picks.reason: Multiple selections and project navigation suit intensive text manipulation in a graphical editor.
picks.tradeoff: Continued use requires a paid license, and deeper IDE features can require plugins.

recipes.title: Pick a Python workspace for learning or analysis
recipes.description: A debugger for learning, an interactive scientific IDE, and notebooks solve different problems.

picks.label: Learn program execution
picks.reason: Its teaching-focused debugger exposes expression evaluation and variable state.
picks.tradeoff: Larger multi-language projects may need a broader development environment.

picks.label: Inspect scientific variables
picks.reason: An IPython console and variable explorer support array and dataframe investigation beside scripts.
picks.tradeoff: Scientific dependencies and environment selection must be kept consistent.

picks.label: Combine code and explanation
picks.reason: Notebooks keep narrative, code, outputs, and data exploration together.
picks.tradeoff: Kernel and execution-order state need discipline for reproducible results.

recipes.title: Review changes and manage Git history
recipes.description: Choose by operating system and preference for a terminal, a guided client, or deeper graphical history tools.

picks.label: Terminal Git workflow
picks.reason: Status, diffs, staging, branches, and rebasing remain accessible from a keyboard-driven interface.
picks.tradeoff: The visual interface does not remove the need to understand history-changing operations.

picks.label: Guided commits
picks.reason: Visual diffs and a focused commit workflow help users review what they are about to commit.
picks.tradeoff: Official distributions support Windows and macOS; advanced Git actions may need the CLI.

picks.label: Windows repository inspection
picks.reason: A commit graph, branch tools, and Windows integration support detailed repository work.
picks.tradeoff: Windows prerequisites and Git configuration still need setup.

picks.label: Paid desktop history tools
picks.reason: Visual interactive rebase, image diffs, and a merge helper suit users who want a dedicated Git GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Windows/macOS only, with a paid license following evaluation.

recipes.title: Build API collections or inspect live HTTP behavior
recipes.description: Sending a request, maintaining a test collection, and intercepting application traffic are distinct tasks.

picks.label: Version API collections
picks.reason: Local plain-text collections can live with the application repository and be reviewed in Git.
picks.tradeoff: Some advanced and team features belong to paid editions.

picks.label: Standalone request CLI
picks.reason: Concise request syntax and formatted responses suit quick terminal investigation.
picks.tradeoff: Not every HTTPie option or behavior is implemented.

picks.label: Inspect and replay traffic
picks.reason: An intercepting proxy with scripting supports repeatable HTTP debugging of authorized targets.
picks.tradeoff: HTTPS interception requires explicit certificate trust and deliberate target configuration.

picks.label: Visual application interception
picks.reason: Application integrations and request filtering help inspect supported HTTP clients through a GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced features and target integrations vary by plan and environment.

recipes.title: Inspect a local database or manage several engines
recipes.description: Start with the database engine and whether the task is browsing, querying, or administration.

picks.label: Local SQLite files
picks.reason: Visual tables and SQL execution let users inspect a SQLite file without a server.
picks.tradeoff: This is a SQLite-focused tool, not a multi-engine administration suite.

picks.label: Several database engines
picks.reason: Drivers, SQL editing, and data browsing share one cross-platform interface.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise and cloud features can differ between Community and paid products.

picks.label: PostgreSQL administration
picks.reason: PostgreSQL-specific object and server tooling provides dedicated administrative context.
picks.tradeoff: It is specialized for PostgreSQL rather than every database engine.

picks.label: Integrated SQL development
picks.reason: Schema-aware SQL and interactive data tools suit database-centric development work.
picks.tradeoff: Free non-commercial eligibility and commercial subscriptions have different conditions.

recipes.title: Choose a local AI interface or inference runtime
recipes.description: Choose the model and memory budget first, then the interface and deployment control you need. No hardware benchmark or model-quality winner is claimed.

picks.label: Managed models and local API
picks.reason: Model management and an application-facing API simplify supported local-model workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Model memory needs, acceleration support, optional cloud use, and model licenses must be checked.

picks.label: Detailed runtime control
picks.reason: Explicit GGUF files and hardware backends suit users who want direct inference configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Build options and supported architectures require more technical decisions.

picks.label: Desktop chat interface
picks.reason: A graphical workspace offers local models alongside configured external providers.
picks.tradeoff: Privacy and cost depend on which provider and model are selected.

picks.label: Questions over documents
picks.reason: Document ingestion and retrieval can be organized into dedicated workspaces.
picks.tradeoff: A local installation can still send data to configured external embedding or model services.

recipes.title: Automate service flows or repetitive typing
recipes.description: Use a flow engine for events and integrations, and a desktop text expander for repeated text. These tools can be complementary.

picks.label: Event and device flows
picks.reason: Visual message flows and reusable nodes support service, API, and device integration.
picks.tradeoff: Installed nodes, credentials, and exposed endpoints require maintenance.

picks.label: Internal service workflows
picks.reason: Visual integration steps and custom code can be combined in hosted or self-hosted workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Its Sustainable Use and enterprise licenses are source-available, with restrictions beyond standard open-source licenses.

picks.label: Connector-based automation
picks.reason: Reusable pieces and visual flows support common service integrations.
picks.tradeoff: Community and enterprise portions use different licensing and features.

picks.label: Cross-application snippets
picks.reason: Typed triggers expand reusable text across supported desktop applications.
picks.tradeoff: Input permissions and application compatibility vary by operating system.

recipes.title: Choose tools for a modded game setup
recipes.description: Match the game and mod ecosystem before choosing a manager; an editor or conflict checker complements deployment rather than replacing it.

picks.label: Profiles and virtual files
picks.reason: Virtual-filesystem deployment separates managed mods from original files for supported games.
picks.tradeoff: Game support and a correct load order still need explicit verification.

picks.label: Nexus-centered workflows
picks.reason: Game extensions, deployment, and profiles integrate with supported Nexus Mods workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extension support, filesystem requirements, and site account features vary.

picks.label: Isolated Minecraft instances
picks.reason: Separate instances organize Minecraft versions, loaders, Java settings, and modpacks.
picks.tradeoff: The game account and all selected Java, loader, and mod versions must be compatible.

picks.label: Bethesda record conflicts
picks.reason: Record-level views reveal plugin conflicts before creating a compatibility patch.
picks.tradeoff: This is a specialist editor; incorrect changes can damage a load order and require backups.

recipes.title: Choose an emulator for the console and title
recipes.description: Console coverage is the first filter. Then consult each project's game compatibility and setup documentation; game and firmware data are separate.

picks.label: GameCube and Wii
picks.reason: Controls and graphics configuration are specialized for GameCube and Wii software.
picks.tradeoff: Per-game compatibility and required controller behavior vary.

picks.label: PlayStation 2
picks.reason: PS2-specific configuration and rendering options support a large range of title-specific setups.
picks.tradeoff: A suitable BIOS and game data are required, and performance depends on the title and hardware.

picks.label: PlayStation 3
picks.reason: The project documents title compatibility and per-game configuration for PS3 emulation.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware demands are substantial for some titles; the official download page was blocked to this research environment.

picks.label: Unified multi-core frontend
picks.reason: A common interface shares controller and display configuration across compatible Libretro cores.
picks.tradeoff: Every core has separate compatibility and licensing; a frontend does not make all consoles equivalent.

recipes.title: Find the source of slow frames or expensive code
recipes.description: Match the measurement tool to the layer being investigated and use a reproducible workload.

picks.label: Rendering pipeline inspection
picks.reason: A captured frame exposes resource contents, shaders, and pipeline state for supported APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Use supported applications and APIs; upstream support is focused on programs you create.

picks.label: Instrumented native programs
picks.reason: CPU, memory, and synchronization events can be correlated on detailed timelines.
picks.tradeoff: Instrumentation needs integration and can influence the measured workload.

picks.label: Correlate system traces
picks.reason: Trace timelines and SQL analysis support multiple event sources in one investigation.
picks.tradeoff: System-wide recording is platform-specific; viewers and analysis tools have broader support.

picks.label: Inspect sampled stacks
picks.reason: Interactive profile views help examine expensive call paths in an imported profile.
picks.tradeoff: It is a viewer, so a separate profiler must first capture compatible data.

recipes.title: Choose a download tool for the transfer type
recipes.description: Select by protocol and automation needs, then use official sources and content you have permission to download.

picks.label: Automated resumable transfers
picks.reason: Several transfer protocols and an RPC interface suit scripted download queues.
picks.tradeoff: Remote-control interfaces need deliberate configuration and access protection.

picks.label: Desktop transfer queue
picks.reason: An aria2-based engine is exposed through a graphical queue.
picks.tradeoff: Site-specific logins or restrictions may need a different workflow.

picks.label: BitTorrent transfers
picks.reason: Desktop and optional web interfaces provide torrent management and transfer controls.
picks.tradeoff: Optional plugins and remote web access introduce additional configuration choices.

picks.label: Permitted media extraction
picks.reason: Site extractors, format selection, and FFmpeg integration support repeatable media workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extractor compatibility changes with websites, and access rights remain separate from technical support.

recipes.title: Choose a browser by workflow and privacy needs
recipes.description: Browser engine, tab organization, defaults, and network routing are separate choices. No browser is claimed universally fastest or safest.

picks.label: Independent browser engine
picks.reason: Gecko and Firefox's extension ecosystem offer an alternative to Chromium-based products.
picks.tradeoff: Test required sites and extensions against the chosen browser and settings.

picks.label: Organize many web tasks
picks.reason: Tab workspaces, tiling, and panels support many concurrent websites in one interface.
picks.tradeoff: The full browser has proprietary terms and more configuration choices.

picks.label: Privacy-oriented defaults
picks.reason: A Firefox-derived configuration includes privacy settings and a content blocker.
picks.tradeoff: Stricter defaults and DRM choices can reduce compatibility with some sites.

picks.label: Tor routing and onion sites
picks.reason: The browser and Tor routing are configured together for a coordinated privacy workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Expect network and site-compatibility tradeoffs; extra plugins or identifying account use can undermine privacy.

recipes.title: Keep recoverable versions of personal files
recipes.description: Choose by operating system, interface preference, and where encrypted backup history will be stored.

picks.label: Open-source CLI fit
picks.reason: Encrypted, versioned backups across supported local and remote storage backends.
picks.tradeoff: Requires command-line setup and an independently tested restore process.

picks.label: Linux and Mac desktop fit
picks.reason: Puts Borg profiles, schedules and archive restoration behind a desktop interface.
picks.tradeoff: Depends on Borg compatibility and does not provide native Windows support.

picks.label: Premium desktop fit
picks.reason: Windows and macOS application for encrypted backups to selected local or cloud destinations.
picks.tradeoff: Software licensing and storage-provider charges may be separate.

recipes.title: Prepare a complete PC recovery image
recipes.description: Disk imaging protects an operating-system installation; keep personal-file backups and restore tests as separate requirements.

picks.label: Graphical boot-media fit
picks.reason: Creates and restores disk images through a GUI with Clonezilla image compatibility.
picks.tradeoff: Requires booting recovery media and selecting the destination carefully.

picks.label: Deployment specialist
picks.reason: Provides disk and partition imaging with specialist deployment workflows.
picks.tradeoff: The boot-media workflow and many options require more familiarity.

picks.label: Premium Windows fit
picks.reason: Integrates Windows image backups and rescue-media recovery.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial edition and subscription terms apply.

recipes.title: Choose a recovery tool by failure type
recipes.description: A failing device, lost partition, and missing file metadata need different tools; recover output to separate storage.

picks.label: Read-error imaging
picks.reason: Copies readable areas of damaged media and records a resumable recovery map.
picks.tradeoff: It copies sectors; it does not reconstruct a lost filesystem or undelete files.

picks.label: Lost-partition specialist
picks.reason: Investigates missing partitions and supported damaged filesystem structures.
picks.tradeoff: Repair modes can modify disk metadata; work from an image when practical.

picks.label: Signature-carving fit
picks.reason: Looks for supported file content even when directory metadata is unusable.
picks.tradeoff: Recovered files can lose their original names and folder layout.

picks.label: Advanced graphical recovery
picks.reason: Offers filesystem reconstruction, disk inspection and RAID-related recovery.
picks.tradeoff: Free-edition limits and advanced editing risks require review.

recipes.title: Find what is consuming disk space
recipes.description: Start with measurement and file review before choosing anything to delete.

picks.label: Windows NTFS specialist
picks.reason: Combines a treemap with Windows NTFS metadata scanning.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial use requires the appropriate license; WizTreeMac has different behavior.

picks.label: Open-source Windows fit
picks.reason: Shows a Windows directory-size breakdown and treemap.
picks.tradeoff: A size visualization does not establish whether a file is disposable.

picks.label: Terminal and SSH fit
picks.reason: Provides interactive directory-size navigation without a graphical desktop.
picks.tradeoff: Permissions limit visibility, and live files may change during a scan.

recipes.title: Manage files across several folders
recipes.description: Compare graphical dual-pane workflows with terminal-first navigation.

picks.label: Open-source dual-pane fit
picks.reason: Offers a commander-style graphical interface across supported desktop platforms.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced operations and plugins still have a learning curve.

picks.label: Premium Windows workflow
picks.reason: Offers extensive Windows file-management customization and automation.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial licensing and configuration effort apply.

picks.label: Terminal workflow fit
picks.reason: Combines asynchronous terminal navigation with configurable file previews.
picks.tradeoff: Preview helpers and terminal image support need compatible setup.

recipes.title: Help someone on a remote computer
recipes.description: Match the connection model to the user’s setup and who operates the coordination service.

picks.label: Self-hosting fit
picks.reason: Supports remote desktop and file transfer with optional self-hosted coordination.
picks.tradeoff: Operating a server and unattended-access policy adds administration.

picks.label: Commercial support fit
picks.reason: Provides a cross-platform remote-support workflow with commercial administration options.
picks.tradeoff: Professional use requires the appropriate license.

picks.label: Linux multi-protocol fit
picks.reason: Collects RDP, VNC and SSH connection profiles in one Linux desktop client.
picks.tradeoff: It needs an existing remote server and suitable protocol plugins.

recipes.title: Connect private devices across networks
recipes.description: Mesh networking connects devices; it is distinct from buying an Internet exit VPN service.

picks.label: Managed coordination fit
picks.reason: Automates private WireGuard-based device connectivity with identity and access policies.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted coordination and plan-specific limits apply.

picks.label: Self-hosted coordination fit
picks.reason: Combines peer networking and access controls with a self-hosting path.
picks.tradeoff: Running the management infrastructure adds operational work.

picks.label: Manual tunnel specialist
picks.reason: Supplies focused encrypted tunnels with explicit peer configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Identity management, discovery and routing must be designed separately.

recipes.title: Replace reused passwords with a vault
recipes.description: Choose between a locally controlled database and a hosted synchronization and sharing workflow.

picks.label: Local encrypted vault
picks.reason: Keeps a cross-platform encrypted password database under the user’s control.
picks.tradeoff: Sync, backups and recovery must be arranged deliberately.

picks.label: Hosted sharing fit
picks.reason: Offers cross-platform vault access and a free entry tier with optional paid sharing features.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced account and organization features vary by plan.

picks.label: Premium shared-vault fit
picks.reason: Provides integrated desktop and browser workflows for family and team vaults.
picks.tradeoff: Requires an ongoing subscription and account recovery planning.

recipes.title: Encrypt files before storing or sharing them
recipes.description: Select a file vault, mounted container, or command-line envelope according to how applications access the data.

picks.label: Cloud-folder fit
picks.reason: Encrypts files individually before a supported sync client uploads the vault.
picks.tradeoff: Cloud synchronization conflicts and separate mobile terms still matter.

picks.label: Mounted-container fit
picks.reason: Lets desktop applications use a mounted encrypted volume.
picks.tradeoff: Container synchronization and recovery planning need care.

picks.label: Scripted-file fit
picks.reason: Encrypts file streams for explicit recipients or a passphrase.
picks.tradeoff: Secret keys and recipients are managed outside a graphical vault.

recipes.title: Run another operating system in a virtual machine
recipes.description: Match host architecture, desired guest, and setup complexity.

picks.label: General desktop lab
picks.reason: Provides a cross-platform graphical VM workflow with snapshots and virtual networks.
picks.tradeoff: Guest architecture support and Extension Pack licensing must be checked.

picks.label: Mac emulation fit
picks.reason: Provides a Mac interface to virtualization and architecture emulation.
picks.tradeoff: Acceleration depends on backend and host/guest architecture.

picks.label: Ubuntu CLI fit
picks.reason: Launches Ubuntu virtual machines with optional cloud-init configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Focused on Ubuntu rather than arbitrary guest operating systems.

picks.label: Simple Linux desktop fit
picks.reason: Offers a streamlined GNOME workflow to download and create desktop guests.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced hypervisor controls are less exposed than in virt-manager.

recipes.title: Inspect hardware before changing settings
recipes.description: Separate component identification, disk health indicators, and stress testing.

picks.label: Windows sensor fit
picks.reason: Combines detailed hardware inventory with sensor monitoring and logging.
picks.tradeoff: Sensor availability is hardware-specific and commercial use has separate terms.

picks.label: Linux report fit
picks.reason: Generates hardware and software information reports with optional benchmark tasks.
picks.tradeoff: Synthetic benchmark results need workload context.

picks.label: Storage-health specialist
picks.reason: Reads supported drive health data and self-test logs through smartctl and smartd.
picks.tradeoff: Controllers can hide data, and a passing health check does not guarantee future reliability.

picks.label: Bootable RAM specialist
picks.reason: Exercises supported system memory outside the installed OS.
picks.tradeoff: Requires boot media and cannot rule out every intermittent hardware problem.

recipes.title: Investigate a slow or unstable network
recipes.description: Measure the path, controlled throughput, and per-process usage separately.

picks.label: Interactive path fit
picks.reason: Shows route-level latency and probe statistics in a terminal.
picks.tradeoff: Intermediate routers can rate-limit replies without dropping application traffic.

picks.label: Controlled throughput fit
picks.reason: Measures a configured client/server network workload.
picks.tradeoff: Needs a test process at both endpoints and is not a speed test of every application.

picks.label: Windows per-app control
picks.reason: Tracks per-application traffic and allows bandwidth rules.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial licensing applies and rules can affect application behavior.

picks.label: Linux per-process view
picks.reason: Groups live bandwidth by the responsible process.
picks.tradeoff: Needs capture privileges and is not a long-term accounting database.
